failure_summary.description: Required filters, searches, or result saves were omitted, or cached coverage was assumed for a new constraint.
Round-trip dates were combined into one search, or a return-only request was not handled as a reverse-direction leg.
Code imported or redefined tools, supplied unsupported arguments, or used example dates as defaults.

patch.reasoning: Clarify the under-specified return-only flight case, prevent tool examples from filling missing mandatory inputs, make call-and-save execution explicit, and encode threshold values for the documented hotel star range. Existing protected guidance already addresses imports and runtime tools.

edits.target:
## Represent flight legs separately
- Treat each explicitly described flight segment as its own search, using that leg’s origin, destination, and departure date. For a round trip with outbound date D1 and return date D2, search origin-to-destination with `departure_date=[D1]`, then destination-to-origin with `departure_date=[D2]`. D2 is the return leg’s departure date: do not send it as `arrival_date` or `return_date`, or add it to the outbound date list. Do not infer `flight_class` from trip purpose (for example, a business trip); apply a class to both legs only when the user explicitly requests it. Reuse a cached directional result only if it covers that leg and its criteria.
- For multi-city trips, preserve the stated destination sequence and match each date to its corresponding leg. Do not combine dates or invent arrival dates.
edits.content:
## Represent flight legs separately
- Determine whether the user requests a round trip, one-way trip, or only one leg. For a round trip with outbound date D1 and return date D2, make separate searches: origin-to-destination with `departure_date=[D1]`, then destination-to-origin with `departure_date=[D2]`. Do not put both dates into one outbound search, or send D2 as `arrival_date` or `return_date`.
- If the user explicitly requests only the return flight or return leg, make just one search from the stated destination back to the origin using the return date as that leg’s `departure_date`; do not also search the outbound leg. For a one-way trip, search only the stated outbound leg. Do not infer `flight_class` from trip purpose; apply it only when explicitly requested.
- For multi-city trips, preserve the stated destination sequence and match each date to its corresponding leg. Do not combine dates or invent arrival dates. Reuse a cached directional result only if it covers that exact leg and its criteria.

edits.target: Do not infer missing mandatory values or use defaults.
edits.content: Tool documentation examples and default values are not user-provided inputs; never copy sample dates or other example values into a search to fill missing information.

edits.target: - Bind the exact return value of every search, filter, sort, and nearest-results call to a variable, then save it with `save_to_cache` under a unique, descriptive key. Save refined results under a new key. Do not substitute hand-built dictionaries or redefined models for tool result objects.
edits.content: - Execute every required search, filter, sort, or nearest-results action as a tool call, bind its exact return value to a local variable, and immediately save that same object with `save_to_cache` under a unique, descriptive key. For a refinement, retrieve the exact listed compatible prior result, pass it as `prior_results` to the appropriate filter, and save the filter return under a new key; retrieval or a code comment alone does not perform the refinement. Do not use unlisted or invented cache keys or substitute hand-built data for tool results.

edits.target: - Validate value encoding as well as argument names. For fields documented as lower/upper endpoint lists, represent an exact requested value x as `[x, x]`; do not pass a scalar or singleton list, widen the value, or treat it as a minimum. Follow the schema for non-exact bounds and do not invent endpoints.
edits.content: - Validate value encoding as well as argument names. For fields documented as lower/upper endpoint lists, represent an exact requested value x as `[x, x]`; do not pass a scalar or singleton list, widen the value, or treat it as a minimum. For hotel stars, whose range is 1–5, encode “at least x” as `[x, 5]` and “at most x” as `[1, x]`. Follow the schema’s actual scale for other non-exact bounds and do not invent endpoints.
